title: Closed localization of a w-contractible ring
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $I\subseteq R$ an ideal, and suppose its closed subset $V(I)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] equals $V(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ for a finite list $f_1,\ldots,f_r\in I$, including $r=0$. Set $S=\{s\in R: s\bmod I\text{ is a unit in }R/I\}$ and $B=S^{-1}R$, the ring of fractions with denominators in $S$. Then $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is a homeomorphism onto the points specializing to $V(I)$, and $B/IB\cong R/I$. The finite family consisting of $\operatorname{Spec}R_{f_k}\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ for $1\leq k\leq r$ and $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is a pro-etale covering [def-weil-pbc-proetale-covering]. If $R$ is w-contractible, meaning every faithfully flat weakly etale ring map $R\to D$ admits an $R$-algebra retraction [def-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ring-map, def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra], then $B$ is w-contractible in the same sense.

proof.text: The set $S$ is multiplicative because the units of $R/I$ contain 1 and are closed under multiplication. The general localization prime correspondence gives a bijection from primes of $B$ to primes $p$ of $R$ disjoint from $S$. Such a $p$ specializes to $V(I)$ exactly when $p+I$ is proper: a proper $p+I$ is contained in a maximal (hence prime) ideal $q$, and then $p\subseteq q$ and $I\subseteq q$; the converse follows from containment in a proper prime. Here maximal ideals are prime because their quotient is a field. Moreover $p+I=R$ implies $1=g+h$ with $g\in p$, $h\in I$, so $g\in S\cap p$. Conversely $s\in S\cap p$ has an inverse modulo $I$, giving $ts+i=1$ for some $t\in R$, $i\in I$, so $p+I=R$. This identifies the image precisely with the asserted specialization set. Specialization in a spectrum is containment of primes: the closure of $\{p\}$ is $V(p)$ directly from the definition of Zariski closed sets.

proof.text: The preceding bijection is a homeomorphism onto its image $H$. Inverse images of $D(a)$ are $D(a/1)$, so it is continuous by the basic-open basis. Every basic open of $\operatorname{Spec}B$ is $D(a/s)=D(a/1)$ since $s$ is a unit. Its image is $H\cap D(a)$, so the bijection is open for the subspace topology, hence its inverse is continuous. This proves the topological clause without using a theorem about the different retained w-localization $R_{[V(I)]}$.

Define $\theta:B\to R/I$ by $a/s\mapsto \bar a\bar s^{-1}$. Fraction equality makes this well-defined: if $u(as'-a's)=0$ with $u\in S$, its reduction can be cancelled since $\bar u$ is a unit. It is a surjective ring map because $a/s$ maps to the reduction of $at$ whenever $st=1\bmod I$. Its kernel is $IB$: $\theta(a/s)=0$ iff $a\in I$, and then $a/s=(a/1)(1/s)\in IB$; every generator of $IB$ maps to zero. Equivalently the maps $B/IB\to R/I$ and $R/I\to B/IB$ given by these fractions and $\bar a\mapsto[a/1]$ are inverse. Thus the isomorphism is the canonical $R$-algebra isomorphism, including the zero quotient.

proof.text: For any localization $R\to L$ at $T$, the localization-flat node makes $L$ flat over $R$. Apply localization base change with $D=L$: $L\to L\otimes_R L$ is localization at the images of $T$, which are already units, so the units-localization node makes it an isomorphism, whose inverse is multiplication. The affine-fibre-product node identifies $\operatorname{Spec}L\times_{\operatorname{Spec}R}\operatorname{Spec}L$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(L\otimes_R L)$, with projections induced by the two tensor inclusions. By affine-spectrum full faithfulness, its diagonal is induced by multiplication: composing multiplication with either inclusion is the identity of $L$. Hence the diagonal of $\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is an isomorphism and is flat (the identity is localization at $\{1\}$). The flat-affine equivalence and the definition of weakly etale imply that every such spectrum map is weakly etale. Apply this to $L=B$ and to all $L=R_{f_k}$. The images $D(f_k)$ together with $H$ cover $\operatorname{Spec}R$: outside $V(I)=V(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ some $f_k$ is not in the prime, while every prime in $V(I)$ belongs to $H$. Each map is between affine schemes and hence affine. For any affine open $V$ of the target its inverse image in every source is therefore affine, and these finitely many inverse images have images whose union is exactly $V$. This verifies the full covering definition, not merely joint surjectivity.

proof.text: Now assume $R$ has the stated retraction property, and take an arbitrary faithfully flat weakly etale map $u:B\to D$. Its spectrum is surjective by the faithfully-flat-surjective-spectrum node. Composition of weakly etale maps makes $\operatorname{Spec}D\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ weakly etale. Replace the $B$-member of the cover in step 4 by $\operatorname{Spec}D$: surjectivity over $\operatorname{Spec}B$ leaves its image $H$ unchanged. All members are affine over the affine target, so their inverse images over every affine open are affine; thus the same finite family is a pro-etale covering. The w-contractible-cover-section node applied to $R$ supplies an $R$-scheme section $\sigma:\operatorname{Spec}R\to P$, where $P=(\coprod_k\operatorname{Spec}R_{f_k})\amalg\operatorname{Spec}D$.

proof.text: Let $h:\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ be the localization map, and consider $\sigma h$. The $D$-summand is open and closed in $P$ by the scheme-coproduct node. Every point of $V(I)$, regarded as a point of $\operatorname{Spec}B$, maps into this summand: $\sigma$ is over $\operatorname{Spec}R$ and no point of $D(f_k)$ lies in $V(I)$ because $f_k\in I$. Every point $x$ of $\operatorname{Spec}B$ specializes to such a point $z$. Indeed step 1 supplies primes $p\subseteq q$ with $q\supseteq I$, both disjoint from $S$, and the corresponding primes $pB\subseteq qB$ give that specialization in $\operatorname{Spec}B$. Continuous maps preserve specialization; membership in a clopen subset is preserved both under specialization and generalization, since both the subset and its complement are closed. Thus all of $\sigma h$ lands in the $D$-summand. Restricting its continuous map and its sheaf morphism to this open subscheme gives a morphism $t:\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}D$ over $\operatorname{Spec}R$. This is an open-subscheme restriction, not factorization through a closed subscheme from containment of point sets.

source.place: Tag 0987, lemma-localization-w-contractible, specialization and summand argument

proof.text: Affine-spectrum full faithfulness turns $t$ into an $R$-algebra map $v:D\to B$. Since it is over $R$, the maps $vu:B\to B$ and $\mathrm{id}_B$ agree on $R$. They agree on all fractions: $vu(a/s)=vu(a/1)vu(s/1)^{-1}=(a/1)(s/1)^{-1}=a/s$. Therefore $vu=\mathrm{id}_B$, as required for the arbitrary map $u$. For $r=0$, the first coproduct is empty and $V(I)=\operatorname{Spec}R$; the argument still applies. For $I=R$, $0\in S$ and $B=0$; its spectrum and every unital $B$-algebra spectrum are empty, and the same constructions give the unique retraction. For $R=0$ all spectra are empty as well. No Noetherian or finite-generation assumption on $I$ was used.
